children: Tesla has always been a Magnificent Seven outlier. Investors should boot it from the list. And what should replace it? SpaceX, naturally.

The Magnificent Seven was coined by BofA strategist Michael Hartnett in 2023, pointing out that they could keep investors safe, referencing the seven cowboys from the famous Western (which referenced the famous Japanese film, Seven Samurai).
Strong balance sheets and cash flow from businesses such as Google Search were better than six-shooters.

Like Chico in the famous Western, Tesla never felt like it belonged in the group. Tesla has built impressive EV and energy storage businesses, but the cash flow potential never matched the rest of the group. Tesla generated record free cash flow in 2022 of about $8 billion. Google owner Alphabet generated $60 billion that year. Apple's free cash flow topped $100 billion.
Then there is valuation. Tesla stock trades at about 180 times earnings estimated over the next 12 months. The rest of the Mag-7 trades at an average of 22 times.

And there are margins. Tesla's operating profit margin in the third quarter was a paltry 2.6%. That was worse than General Motors' 8.2% margin. Nvidia's projected third-quarter operating profit margin is 66%.

SpaceX fits the group better. It isn't generating free cash now, but neither is Alphabet. Both are spending heavily on AI. But SpaceX has its cash cow: its space-based broadband business, Starlink, that serves more than 13 million customers in more than 170 countries using more than 11,000 satellites. Starlink's third-quarter operating profit margin was 45%.

SpaceX stock also trades at about 40 times estimated earnings expected over the coming 12 months, a small premium to Apple. (SpaceX trades at a discount to Apple based on calendar year 2027 earnings, according to FactSet.)

AI, low-valuation, and cash-generating business segment — SpaceX fits the bill. There is, of course, no official criteria for being a Magnificent Seven stock. Someone, eventually, will coin the Great Eight.

Tesla might not be in that one, either. Not because of problems with the Tesla business, but because Tesla and SpaceX are likely to merge. Analysts and investors have speculated about a deal for months, and CEO (of both companies) Elon Musk said in October that both boards were evaluating a combination.

Conventional wisdom says that SpaceX is the acquirer paying some premium in an all-stock deal. Depending on the day, three shares of SpaceX for one share of Tesla would mean Tesla shareholders end up owning roughly 49% of the combined company (on a fully diluted basis).
In that scenario, SpaceX-Tesla would be valued at about $4 trillion (on a fully diluted basis) and trade for about 65 times 2027 earnings, with roughly 85% of earnings coming from SpaceX.

Time will tell if Tesla and SpaceX investors will agree to that, or another, ratio. Congress shouldn't get in the way, despite the Democratic sweep. Deutsche Bank analyst Edison Yu wrote recently that he doesn't see Congress interfering with the job of the Federal Trade Commission and Justice Department. Those two entities approve mergers.

"With Elon Musk having provided significant financial support to the Republicans, we think there is a perception of potential political retribution," added Yu. "While there are ways for Congress to interfere, nearly all dealings are conducted with executive-branch agencies."
Tesla's days in the ranks of the Mag-7 tech giants might be numbered. Like Chico from the Western, Tesla will survive. It will likely be part of a much larger entity after combining with SpaceX.
